questions.question: An ambulance service tightens fingerprint sign-in on its crews' patient-record tablets so impostors are almost never accepted. Which side effect should the IT team MOST expect?

options.A: More genuine crew members turned away by the reader
options.B: Fewer repeat scans needed by genuine crew members
options.C: A higher crossover error rate for each reader
options.D: Copied fingerprints no longer working for the attackers

questions.key_concept: Tightening a biometric threshold lowers false acceptances but raises false rejections; the two errors trade against each other.
questions.pre_read: Picture both kinds of people at a tablet: crew members and impostors.
questions.correct_explanation: Every biometric reader trades two errors. Lowering false acceptances (false matches), where an impostor matches, raises false rejections (false non-matches), where a genuine crew member fails to match. So crews will be turned away more often and need a quick fallback during a call. Expecting copied fingerprints to fail is the runner-up: the threshold judges ordinary impostors, while stopping fakes needs presentation attack detection.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a stricter reader sounds more accurate. But tightening works the other way: genuine fingers that matched before now fall short, so crews need more repeat scans.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it names a real biometric measure. But the crossover rate is where both errors meet for a reader; moving the threshold does not change it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a stricter reader sounds harder to fool. But a good copy of an enrolled fingerprint still matches; spotting fakes needs presentation attack detection, such as liveness checks.

tips: Eliminate: B reverses the trade-off, since a stricter match sends genuine users back to rescan, and C confuses a reader's fixed crossover point with its threshold setting.
Final two: A beats D because the threshold sets how close a match must be; copied fingerprints are stopped by presentation attack detection, not by tightening.
Exam cue: biometrics balance false acceptance against false rejection. Push one down and the other rises, so plan a fallback for genuine users.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.3 (Use of Biometrics: false match and false non-match rates)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'biometric thresholds trade false acceptances against false rejections' (notes 3.1.4 Authentication Factors and MFA). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): runner-up is D (copied prints), B no longer falls on an absolute, terms match the cited source.

questions.question: A newspaper moves staff sign-in to passkeys, but keeps a password plus a texted code as an option anyone can pick. Which attack should its IT team MOST expect?

options.A: Thieves reading texted codes on staff phones they have stolen
options.B: Attackers guessing the short PIN that unlocks each passkey
options.C: Attackers copying private keys stored on the newspaper's server
options.D: Look-alike pages steering staff to the texted-code fallback

questions.key_concept: Phishing resistance holds only if attackers cannot steer users to a weaker method; a texted-code option reopens the relay.
questions.pre_read: List each way staff can now sign in, and what an attacker would need for each.
questions.correct_explanation: Passkeys stop a fake page from reusing a sign-in, but only when staff must use them. While anyone can pick a texted code, a fake page simply asks for the password and code and relays both to the real site. A stolen phone is the runner-up: texted codes reach whoever holds it, but a thief still needs the password, and theft hits one person at a time.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: texted codes do reach whoever holds the phone. But a thief still needs the password, and theft hits one person; a fake page collects both from many.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because PINs are short. But the PIN only unlocks the passkey on the user's own device; it never reaches the site, so remote guessing fails.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because servers do get breached. But the site holds only public keys; private keys stay with the user, so a breach yields nothing to sign in with.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes the unlocking PIN reaches the site, and C assumes the server holds private keys; passkeys keep both with the user.
Final two: D beats A because a fake page collects the password and code together from many staff; a thief must also know the password.
Exam cue: sign-in is only as phishing-resistant as the weakest method users may pick. Remove or restrict the fallback, or attackers will steer users to it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.5 (Phishing Resistance: manually entered codes can be relayed by an impostor verifier); NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.2.5.2 (Verifier Name Binding)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a weaker fallback beside passkeys reopens phishing' (notes 3.1.5 Phishing-Resistant MFA and Passkeys). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Re-angled 31 Oct 2026 (cross-domain review CD-11): the earlier version asked why passkeys resist a look-alike page, which duplicated cc_d3_002; it now tests the risk of a weaker fallback. Fix-up 31 Oct 2026 (audit): 'staff' now appears in A as well as D, and D no longer repeats the stem word 'sign-in'. Fix-up round 2, 31 Oct 2026 (blind test and audit): the stem now asks which attack to expect, matching the options, and D steers staff to the whole fallback, so the fake page collects the password as well as the code.

questions.question: An online bookshop's developer plans to store customer passwords encrypted, so support staff can read forgotten ones back to customers. Which approach should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt them and have the support lead approve each lookup
options.B: Store salted, slow hashes and offer a verified password reset
options.C: Encode the passwords in Base64 so they look unreadable
options.D: Store the passwords as fast SHA-256 hashes to keep sign-in quick

questions.key_concept: Store passwords as salted, slow hashes and reset forgotten ones; never keep them in a form that can be read back.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an attacker who steals the stored passwords could do under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Anything that can be decrypted can be stolen and read, so passwords are stored as salted hashes, using a slow hashing scheme that makes each guess costly. A forgotten password is replaced through a verified reset, never read back. Encrypting with lead-approved lookups is the runner-up: it limits who reads passwords, but a stolen key or an insider still exposes every one.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an approval step limits who reads passwords. But anything decryptable can be stolen and read; a stolen key or an insider still exposes every one.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the stored text looks scrambled. But Base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone can reverse it instantly without a key.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because SHA-256 is a strong, well-known hash. But it is built to be fast, so attackers who steal the file can test enormous numbers of guesses quickly.

tips: Eliminate: C uses reversible encoding, not protection, and D uses SHA-256, a strong but fast hash, so a stolen file is quick to crack.
Final two: B beats A because hashes cannot be turned back into passwords; anything encrypted can be decrypted by whoever gets the key.
Exam cue: passwords are never recovered, only reset. Store them salted and slow-hashed so a stolen file is costly to crack.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: password requirements); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5(1) (Authenticator Management | Password-based Authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'store passwords as salted, slow hashes and reset rather than recover them' (notes 3.1.6 Passwords and Modern Password Standards). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Fix-up 31 Oct 2026 (audit): D now shares the verb 'store' with the key, and the explanation no longer says an approval step limits who can decrypt. Fix-up round 2, 31 Oct 2026 (blind test and audit): D now names SHA-256, testing the belief that a strong, well-known hash is good enough for passwords, and the key is no longer the longest option.

questions.question: A school's developer is adding 'Sign in with your school account' to a homework app, which must learn who each student is. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Use OpenID Connect and verify the ID token it returns
options.B: Use OAuth 2.0 and verify the access token it returns
options.C: Treat each student's school email address as proof of identity
options.D: Have students type their school password into the app

questions.key_concept: OpenID Connect proves who a user is with a signed ID token; OAuth 2.0 alone grants access to data, not identity.
questions.pre_read: Focus on what the app needs to learn, and which option actually gives it that.
questions.correct_explanation: OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity to OAuth 2.0: the school's identity provider signs an ID token saying who the student is, and the app checks it. An OAuth 2.0 access token alone is the runner-up: it lets an app reach data on a user's behalf, but it is not built to prove who the user is.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: OpenID Connect is built on OAuth 2.0. But an access token grants limited access to data; it is not designed to prove who the user is.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because each address belongs to one student. But an address is only a claim; anyone can type it, so it proves nothing on its own.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it checks a real password. But federated sign-in exists so the app never sees the password; collecting it invites theft.

tips: Eliminate: D hands the password to the app, which federation avoids, and C treats a claimed address as proof.
Final two: A beats B because the ID token proves who signed in; an OAuth access token only grants access to data.
Exam cue: OAuth 2.0 grants access; OpenID Connect adds identity on top. For 'who is this user?', look for OpenID Connect or SAML.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63C-4 Section 3.12.3 (Identity APIs: the ID Token is the assertion and an OAuth 2.0 access token reaches the API)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'OpenID Connect proves identity while OAuth 2.0 grants access' (notes 3.1.7 Single Sign-On and Federation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A claims handler at an insurer moves to underwriting, and the claims manager asks that they keep claims access for two weeks to hand over open files. What is the access analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Keep the claims access until the handler confirms handovers are done
options.B: Ask the underwriting manager to approve keeping the old access
options.C: Record the claims access as temporary, with an end date
options.D: Keep the claims access, since both teams belong to the insurer

questions.key_concept: When a mover needs old access for a handover, grant it as approved, temporary access that expires on a set date.
questions.pre_read: Note what the claims manager asked for and for how long.
questions.correct_explanation: Handover access is a real need, but it must be approved for a set period and then expire, or the mover keeps old rights indefinitely. Recording it as temporary with a two-week end date meets the need and removes it automatically. Keeping it until the handler says they are done is the runner-up: it depends on someone remembering, and leftover access tends to stay.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it allows for handovers. But with no end date, removal depends on someone remembering, and leftover rights become privilege creep.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the new manager approves new access. But the claims manager decides about claims access, and this keeps the old access with no end date.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both teams sit inside one company. But access follows the job, not the employer; old rights the new job does not need should go.

tips: Eliminate: D ties access to the employer instead of the job, and B asks the wrong manager to approve old access with no end date.
Final two: C beats A because an end date removes the access automatically; waiting for the handler's word lets it linger.
Exam cue: movers lose old access at the move. If a handover needs some of it, grant it as temporary access with an end date.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-5 (Personnel Transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'handover access for a mover is approved separately and expires' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A departing developer owns the service account a nightly sales report uses, and knows its password; the report must keep running. What should the IT technician arrange as BEST?

options.A: Write the password into the handover notes for the team
options.B: Disable the service account along with its departing owner's login
options.C: Leave the service account alone, since nobody signs in with it
options.D: Assign the account a new owner, who then changes its password

questions.key_concept: A leaver's service accounts need a new owner and changed secrets if still needed, or retirement if not.
questions.pre_read: Note the two facts about the service account, and weigh each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: A service account outlives its owner's job, so it needs a new named owner. Because the developer knows the password, the new owner changes it, so the leaver's knowledge stops working. Disabling it is the runner-up: it would close the risk, but it breaks a report the business still needs; retiring an account is right only when nothing needs it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the team will need it. But a password in shared notes spreads the secret further; it belongs in a vault with a named owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: removing the leaver's access is the goal. But the report must keep running, so disabling breaks it; a new owner and new password close the risk instead.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because no person signs in with it. But the developer still knows a working password, and ownerless service accounts are a favorite target.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a password the leaver knows working, and A spreads the secret instead of protecting it.
Final two: D beats B because the report must keep running; a new owner and new password remove the leaver's access without breaking it.
Exam cue: when someone leaves, check what they owned and knew, not just their own login. Reassign and rotate what is still needed; retire the rest.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'a leaver's service accounts are reassigned and rotated, or retired' (notes 3.1.12 Non-Human Identities Through the Life Cycle; 3.1.11 Deprovisioning Leavers). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A council's role-based system has 380 roles for 400 staff, mostly one-offs created for single requests, though staff fall into about 15 job types. Which fix should the access analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Consolidate into standard roles, adding time-limited extras
options.B: Keep the custom roles and review each one yearly
options.C: Replace the roles with attribute-based access control
options.D: Let managers edit their own team's roles whenever needed

questions.key_concept: Role-based access control works when roles mirror jobs; one-off needs are temporary requests, not new custom roles.
questions.pre_read: Compare the number of roles with the number of job types, and ask what that gap means.
questions.correct_explanation: Role-based access control works when roles match jobs; hundreds of one-off roles defeat it and make reviews and moves hard. With about 15 job types, rebuilding job roles and handling one-off needs as time-limited requests restores order. Attribute-based control is the runner-up: it answers role explosion caused by many changing conditions, such as location or training, but these roles came from single requests.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reviews catch excess access. But reviewing 380 near-duplicate roles each year is the burden sprawl creates; it leaves the sprawl in place.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: attribute-based control is a known remedy for role explosion. But it suits changing conditions; these roles came from single requests, and access follows 15 job types.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because managers know their teams. But unreviewed edits by each manager are how roles multiplied, and no owner checks them for conflicts.

tips: Eliminate: D keeps the unchecked edits that caused the sprawl, and B reviews the 380 roles instead of reducing them.
Final two: A beats C because access here follows job type, which is what roles express; attribute rules add complexity this case does not need.
Exam cue: when roles outnumber jobs, rebuild roles around jobs and handle one-off needs as time-limited requests.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'roles should mirror jobs, with one-off needs handled as temporary requests' (notes 3.2.7 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. Standards audit fix (30 Oct 2026): stem now says why the roles exist, so attribute-based control is no longer defensible; B is no longer a strawman.

questions.question: A junior network administrator finds 140 allow rules, many with no recorded purpose, on the firewall guarding a clinic's lab systems, which the network manager owns. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Move the unexplained rules to the end of the rule list
options.B: Write a purpose for each rule from its recent traffic logs
options.C: List the rules and ask the manager to arrange a review
options.D: Disable the unexplained rules now, then tell the manager

questions.key_concept: Access rules pile up over time; each needs an owner, a purpose and periodic review, arranged through the system's owner.
questions.pre_read: Note what the administrator found and who owns the device.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules pile up, and each needs an owner, a purpose and a periodic review. The administrator's part is to document the rules and bring them to the firewall's owner, who can arrange a review with each business area. Disabling unexplained rules is the runner-up: they may look unused, but some may carry live lab traffic, and changing the firewall is the owner's decision, made through change control.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rules at the end are matched last. But reordering an owned firewall's rules is still a change; it can break live lab traffic and skips the owner.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recorded purposes are the goal. But traffic shows what a rule carries, not why it should exist; only the owner can confirm each purpose.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: unexplained rules are a real risk. But some may carry live lab traffic, and changes to an owned firewall go through its owner and change control.

tips: Eliminate: A reorders an owned firewall's rules without change control, and B guesses purposes from traffic that only the owner can confirm.
Final two: C beats D because the manager owns the firewall; the administrator documents and raises the issue rather than changing live rules alone.
Exam cue: every access rule needs an owner, a purpose and a review. Report rule sprawl to the owner; do not clean it up alone.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 Section 5.5 (Manage: review the firewall policy regularly to find rules no longer needed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)

Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026. questions.question: A 30-person design agency gives staff access by job, and its owner wants to switch to mandatory access control because it is the strictest model. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Use mandatory access control, because the strictest model is the safest
options.B: Use role-based access control, because each job maps to one role
options.C: Use rule-based access control, because one rule can cover every job
options.D: Use discretionary access control, because owners know their own files best

questions.key_concept: Choose an access control model that fits the data and the organization; the strictest model is not automatically the best.
questions.pre_read: Note what the agency handles and how access works today, then judge each model's fit.
questions.correct_explanation: The best model fits the data and the organization, not the strictest one available. A design agency whose access already follows jobs suits role-based access control. Mandatory access control is the runner-up: it is strong, but its central labels and clearances are rigid and costly, built for classified data, and would slow a small creative team for little gain.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: mandatory control is the strictest. But labels and clearances are rigid and costly, suited to classified data, not a small agency's artwork.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rules are simple. But one rule applies to everyone alike, so it cannot give designers and accountants different access.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners know their files. But discretionary control lets each owner share at will, inviting oversharing, and moves away from job-based access.

tips: Eliminate: D hands access decisions to each owner, inviting oversharing, and C applies one condition to everyone, so it cannot reflect different jobs.
Final two: B beats A because the model should fit the data and size; mandatory control's labels suit classified data, not a design agency.
Exam cue: choose the model by who should decide and what the data needs; the strictest model is not automatically the best.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(7) (Access Enforcement | Role-based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'choose the model that fits the data and organization, not the strictest' (notes 3.2.10 Choosing an Access Control Model). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A school's IT technician must give 25 new teachers edit access to the shared lesson-plan folder. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Grant each teacher edit rights on the folder one by one
options.B: Share the folder with everyone so no teacher is missed
options.C: Give the teachers one shared login that has the folder rights
options.D: Add the teachers to a group that holds the folder rights

questions.key_concept: Grant permissions to groups or roles and manage membership, so access stays easy to review and remove.
questions.pre_read: Think ahead to the day one of these teachers leaves, and what each option leaves behind.
questions.correct_explanation: Permissions are best granted to groups, not individuals. Adding the teachers to a group that holds the folder rights gives the same access, and when a teacher leaves or changes job, removing them from the group removes the access. Granting rights one by one is the runner-up: it works today, but 25 separate entries are hard to review and easy to leave behind.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it gives the right access today. But 25 separate entries are hard to review, and each must be found and removed when a teacher moves.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because nobody is left out. But everyone includes pupils, office staff and visitors, far beyond the teachers who need the folder.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one login is quick to set up. But a shared login hides which teacher made each change and cannot be removed for one person.

tips: Eliminate: B opens the folder to far more people than need it, and C puts every teacher on one login that cannot show who acted.
Final two: D beats A because group membership is easy to review and remove; individual grants pile up and get missed.
Exam cue: grant rights to groups or roles, then manage who belongs. It keeps reviews and removals simple.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'grant permissions to groups or roles rather than individuals' (notes 3.2.1 Logical Access Controls and Access Decisions). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a tax office, case officers can open any taxpayer's file, and one officer browsed a famous athlete's file with no assigned case. Which change should the office manager make to BEST prevent this?

options.A: Limit each officer to files for their assigned cases
options.B: Remove the officers' rights to edit any file
options.C: Log each file viewed and check it against assigned cases monthly
options.D: Require multifactor sign-in before officers open any file

questions.key_concept: Need to know limits each person to the information their current work requires, preventing curiosity browsing.
questions.pre_read: Picture the same officer trying the same lookup after each change.
questions.correct_explanation: Need to know limits each person to the information their current work requires. Tying access to assigned cases stops browsing before it happens. Logging views and checking them against assigned cases is the runner-up: it would catch the officer afterward and deters misuse, but the athlete's privacy is already breached by then.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it limits what officers can do. But browsing is reading, so officers without edit rights can still view every file.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: logging deters and detects browsing. But it acts after the file has been seen, and the goal is to prevent it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it strengthens access. But it proves who the officer is; it does not limit which files they may open.

tips: Eliminate: B limits changes, not viewing, and D strengthens sign-in without limiting which files open.
Final two: A beats C because it stops the browsing before it happens; logs only reveal it afterward.
Exam cue: need to know asks whether this person's current work requires this data. When asked to prevent, pick the preventive control over the detective one.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3 (Access Enforcement)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'need to know limits people to the data their current work requires' (notes 3.2.2 Least Privilege and Need to Know). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: At a water utility, two operators staff each shift, and either can change chlorine dosing from the control room; a wrong level could harm the public. Which control should the plant manager add as BEST?

options.A: Require a longer password for the operator's account
options.B: Log each dosing change and alert the supervisor
options.C: Require a second operator to confirm each dosing change
options.D: Rotate dosing duties among the operators every week

questions.key_concept: Two-person control requires a second authorized person to confirm a high-impact action before it takes effect.
questions.pre_read: Note what could happen to people if one wrong change went through.
questions.correct_explanation: When a single wrong action could hurt people, a second authorized person should confirm it before it takes effect: two-person control. Logging with an alert is the runner-up: it records who acted and brings help quickly, but it works after the chlorine level has changed, when harm may already be under way. Prevention comes first where public safety is at stake.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it strengthens sign-in. But it proves who the operator is; it does not stop that operator acting alone.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: alerts bring a fast response. But they fire after the level changes, and harm to the public may already have started.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because job rotation is a real control. But it helps uncover misuse over time; on any given shift, one operator can still make a harmful change alone.

tips: Eliminate: D changes who acts alone rather than adding a second person, and A strengthens sign-in without stopping a lone change.
Final two: C beats B because confirmation happens before the change takes effect; an alert comes after people may already be at risk.
Exam cue: for high-impact actions, especially where safety is at stake, require a second person before the action, not a log after it.

questions.question: A TV broadcaster's vendor engineer will upgrade its playout server remotely and unsupervised, with administrator rights. Which control should the system administrator set up to BEST show the owner exactly what the engineer did?

options.A: Log when the engineer's admin account signs in and out
options.B: Record the engineer's session in the privileged access tool
options.C: Ask the engineer for a written summary of every change
options.D: Let the engineer use the IT team's shared admin account

questions.key_concept: Privileged sessions, especially by outsiders, should be brokered and recorded so the owner can see exactly what was done.
questions.pre_read: Ask what evidence each option would give the owner the next morning.
questions.correct_explanation: Privileged access management can broker an outsider's admin session and record it, so the owner can replay exactly what was done. Logging sign-in and sign-out is the runner-up: it shows when the engineer was on the server, but not which commands they ran or which settings they changed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it shows when the engineer was connected. But sign-in times reveal nothing about which commands or settings were changed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the engineer knows what they did. But a self-written summary can leave things out; it is not independent evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is quick to arrange. But a shared account hides who acted, so the engineer's actions mix with the IT team's.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on the engineer's own account of events, and D mixes the engineer's actions into a shared login.
Final two: B beats A because a session recording shows what was done; sign-in logs show only when someone arrived and left.
Exam cue: for privileged work, especially by outsiders, record the session itself; sign-in records prove presence, not actions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-14 (Session Audit); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MA-4 (Nonlocal Maintenance)

questions.question: A publishing house's project lead gives an editor full control of a manuscripts folder to revise, and the editor reshares it with a freelancer. Which change should the project lead make to BEST prevent this?

options.A: Ask the freelancer to confirm they deleted the manuscripts
options.B: Give the editor read access in place of full control
options.C: Share the folder by link instead of by name
options.D: Give the editor edit rights that do not include sharing

questions.key_concept: Under discretionary access control, holders of full control can pass access on, so grant only the rights each person needs.
questions.pre_read: Trace how the manuscripts reached the freelancer, step by step.
questions.correct_explanation: Under discretionary access control, whoever holds full control can pass access on. Edit rights without the right to share let the editor do the job while sharing decisions stay with the owner. Read access is the runner-up: it would stop the reshare, but an editor must change the manuscripts, so it blocks the work the access exists for.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it seems to undo the share. But copies may already exist, and nothing stops the next onward share.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: read access would stop the reshare. But the editor must change the manuscripts, so read access blocks their job; edit rights without sharing fit it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because links feel tidy. But anyone who obtains a link can open the folder, which widens sharing instead of limiting it.

tips: Eliminate: A tries to undo one share after the fact, and C widens access to anyone holding the link.
Final two: D beats B because the editor needs to change the manuscripts; edit rights without sharing fit the job, while read access blocks it.
Exam cue: in discretionary access control, full control includes passing access on. Grant the rights the job needs, and keep sharing with the owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(4) (Access Enforcement | Discretionary Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'under DAC, full control lets holders pass access on, so limit sharing rights' (notes 3.2.5 Discretionary Access Control (DAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: Under mandatory access control, an analyst cleared to Top Secret is refused a Top Secret file belonging to another program. What MOST likely explains the refusal?

options.A: The analyst's clearance must be one level above the label
options.B: The file's owner has not shared it with the analyst
options.C: The file's compartment requires a need to know the analyst lacks
options.D: Top Secret files need the security officer to open them

questions.key_concept: Mandatory access control needs both a sufficient clearance and a need to know, often enforced through compartments.
questions.pre_read: Note what the analyst holds and what the file belongs to.
questions.correct_explanation: Under mandatory access control, clearance is necessary but not sufficient. Files are often placed in compartments, and the system also checks that the person has a need to know for that compartment, so a Top Secret clearance alone does not open another program's work. The owner not sharing is the runner-up: owner choice is how discretionary control works; under mandatory control, owners cannot grant access at will.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because higher sounds safer. But a clearance equal to the label is enough; the extra check is need to know, not a higher level.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: someone did withhold access. But owner choice is discretionary control; under mandatory control, central labels and need to know decide, not the owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Top Secret sounds reserved for officers. But cleared staff with a need to know can open such files; the officer manages labels.

tips: Eliminate: A invents a rule that clearance must exceed the label, and D wrongly reserves Top Secret files for the security officer.
Final two: C beats B because mandatory control checks label, clearance and need to know; owners do not decide.
Exam cue: under mandatory access control, a matching clearance is necessary but not enough; need to know, often by compartment, is the second test.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(3) (Access Enforcement | Mandatory Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-16 (Security and Privacy Attributes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'under MAC, clearance is necessary but need to know is also required' (notes 3.2.6 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A firm's attribute-based policy opens sales files only to staff whose department attribute is Sales, yet a worker who moved to finance weeks ago still opens them. Which cause should the analyst MOST suspect?

options.A: The worker still holds a Sales role in the directory
options.B: The department attribute at its source still says Sales
options.C: The policy checked the department attribute once, at account creation
options.D: The worker's multifactor sign-in was not re-enrolled after the move

questions.key_concept: Attribute-based access control is only as accurate as its attributes; a stale value at the source gives a wrong decision.
questions.pre_read: Note exactly what the policy checks, then ask where that value comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute-based control decides each request from current attribute values, so it is only as accurate as its attributes. If the attribute's source, such as the human resources record, still lists Sales, the policy correctly applies to a wrong value and grants access. A leftover Sales role is the runner-up: it would matter under role-based control, but this policy checks the department attribute, not roles.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: leftover roles often cause privilege creep. But this policy checks the department attribute, not role membership, so a role alone would not open the files.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some attributes are set at hiring. But attribute-based control evaluates attributes on every request, so changes should take effect.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the worker's situation changed. But sign-in proves identity; it does not decide which files the policy allows.

tips: Eliminate: C misdescribes the model, which checks attributes on each request, and D confuses sign-in with the access decision.
Final two: B beats A because the policy reads the department attribute; a stale value grants access whatever roles say.
Exam cue: attribute-based decisions are only as good as their attributes. When access is wrong but the policy is right, suspect stale data at the source.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-162 Section 3.2.3.1 (Confidence in Access Control Decisions: accurate and timely attributes from authoritative sources); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-3(13) (Access Enforcement | Attribute-based Access Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ABAC decisions are only as accurate as their attributes' (notes 3.2.8 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: A firm's AI assistant answers staff questions by searching all file shares through its own all-access account, so interns can get answers drawn from payroll files. Which fix should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Limit it to files that the person asking can already open
options.B: Require interns to use multifactor sign-in before asking it
options.C: Block any answer that mentions salaries or other payroll terms
options.D: Keep its access, since reading files changes nothing

questions.key_concept: An AI assistant acting for a user should reach only what that user may access; filtering output does not fix excess access.
questions.pre_read: Trace how payroll details reached an intern, step by step.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI assistant should never reach more than the person it is acting for. Limiting each search to files the asking person can already open closes the gap. Blocking payroll words is the runner-up: it hides one obvious leak, but other sensitive files, and differently worded answers, still pass through the all-access account.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it strengthens sign-in. But it confirms who the intern is; it does not limit which files the assistant searches for them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it hides the most obvious leak. But word filters miss other sensitive files and rephrased answers, and the all-access account remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reading changes nothing. But reading is exactly how payroll data reached interns; read access to everything breaks least privilege.

tips: Eliminate: D treats read-only access as harmless, and B strengthens sign-in without limiting what the assistant can reach.
Final two: A beats C because it removes the excess access itself; a word filter only masks some of what the account can still reach.
Exam cue: an AI agent acting for a user should never reach more than that user can. Fix the access, not just the output.
questions.framework_ref: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 LLM06 (Excessive Agency); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'an AI agent never reaches more than the user it acts for' (notes 3.2.11 Least Privilege and SoD for Automated Systems and AI Agents). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A retailer's administrators all sign in through single sign-on (SSO), and the IT manager wants an emergency account for when SSO itself fails. Which setup should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Assign it to the IT manager as a second everyday admin account
options.B: Give it a strong password that rotates monthly
options.C: Protect it with SSO and multifactor authentication, and alert on each use
options.D: Keep its credentials sealed offline and alert on each use

questions.key_concept: Break-glass accounts must work when normal sign-in fails: sealed credentials, few holders, regular tests and an alert on every use.
questions.pre_read: Note what the emergency account is for, and what each setup depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: A break-glass account must work when normal sign-in fails, so it cannot depend on SSO. Its credentials are sealed offline, such as in a safe, held by few people and tested regularly, and every use raises an alert and a review. Putting it behind SSO with multifactor authentication is the runner-up: that suits daily admin accounts, but it would fail in exactly the outage it exists for.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one named person is accountable. But daily use exposes it to the same attacks as normal accounts; an emergency account stays unused until needed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rotation sounds safe. But routine rotation misses its purpose: few should hold it, it stays sealed, and every use raises an alert.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: strong sign-in suits admin accounts. But if it depends on SSO, it fails in the very outage it exists for; use a strong factor that works without SSO.

tips: Eliminate: A turns the emergency account into an everyday one, and B treats it like any admin account instead of sealing it and watching its use.
Final two: D beats C because the account must work when SSO fails; tying it to SSO defeats its purpose.
Exam cue: break-glass access is sealed, independent of the system that might fail, tested, and alerts on every use.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2(12) (Account Management | Account Monitoring for Atypical Usage)

Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 2, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Identity life cycle. Identities and accounts
questions.question: A film studio disables leavers in its central directory the same day, but their logins on three stand-alone editing systems, tracked nowhere else, often stay active. What should the IT analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Link every editing-system login to the person's identity record
options.B: Have each editing system's administrator keep a separate staff list
options.C: Disable any editing-system login left unused for 45 days
options.D: Review the editing-system logins against HR records each year

questions.key_concept: Every account should trace to one known identity, so a single trusted event can find and remove all of a person's access.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the leaver process would find each login a person holds.
questions.correct_explanation: Every account should belong to one known identity, so the leaver trigger can find all of a person's access. Linking each editing-system login to the person's identity record lets the same-day leaver process reach those systems too. Disabling logins unused for 45 days is the runner-up: it is a useful backstop for dormant accounts, but it leaves a leaver's access live for weeks and never fixes why removal misses them.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because local administrators know their own systems. But separate lists drift from HR records, and nothing connects them to the leaver event.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a dormant-account rule is a good backstop. But a leaver's login stays usable for up to 45 days, and removal still misses these systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because reviews catch leftover accounts. But a yearly check leaves a leaver's login live for up to a year; the leaver process itself must reach these systems.

tips: Eliminate: B splits the record into lists that drift from HR, and D waits up to a year for a review to catch what the leaver process should remove.
Final two: A beats C because a login linked to the identity is removed by the same-day leaver process; an idle rule waits 45 days.
Exam cue: every account belongs to one known identity, so one trusted event, such as an HR exit, can find and remove all of it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-4 (Personnel Termination)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'every account belongs to a known identity, so one trusted trigger reaches all of it' (notes 3.1.1 Identities, Accounts and the Life Cycle). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A botanical garden is moving to a new booking system and must define its 'ticket desk' role before any staff are added. Which starting point should the IT analyst use as BEST?

options.A: The access held today by the longest-serving desk worker
options.B: The old system's ticket desk role, copied over unchanged
options.C: The desk's current tasks and the permissions each task needs
options.D: Full access at launch, trimmed after a month of usage

questions.key_concept: A role is built from the job's tasks and the permissions each task needs, then approved by the owner.
questions.pre_read: Think about where each starting point's permissions came from.
questions.correct_explanation: Roles come from duties: list what the job does, then the permissions each task needs, and have the owner approve the result. Copying the old system's role is the runner-up: it looks like a ready-made definition, but old roles collect rights over the years and may not map to the new system, so it carries old excess forward instead of checking it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because that worker knows the job well. But long service often means leftover rights from past duties, so copying them spreads excess access.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the old role is a quick template. But it may carry years of extra rights and may not match the new system's permissions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because usage data looks objective. But full access is live from day one, and trimming later rarely happens.

tips: Eliminate: A copies one person's accumulated rights, and D grants everything first and plans to trim later, which leaves excess access live.
Final two: C beats B because a role built from today's tasks holds only what the job needs; an old role carries old excess forward.
Exam cue: define a role from the job's tasks, not from a coworker, an old system or usage after the fact.
questions.framework_ref: CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.8 (Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'roles are defined from the job's tasks, not copied from existing access' (notes 3.1.2 Defining Roles and Entitlements). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A language school's HR system sends a start record for a teacher beginning in three weeks, and procedure has the IT technician prepare accounts on receipt. What is the technician's BEST action?

options.A: Create and enable it now, sending the teacher a unique password
options.B: Create the account now, but keep it disabled until day one
options.C: Create the account with the access of the teacher being replaced
options.D: Create the account with the standard first password for new hires

questions.key_concept: Provision from the HR record, with unique first credentials and the approved role, and enable access only when the person starts.
questions.pre_read: Think about who could use each account during the three weeks before the teacher arrives.
questions.correct_explanation: Provisioning from the HR record is right, but an account enabled weeks early is live access nobody needs yet. Creating it now and enabling it on the start date gives the teacher working access on day one without that gap. Enabling it now with a unique password is the runner-up: unique first credentials are right, but the account goes live weeks early, usable by anyone who obtains that password.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: unique first passwords are right. But the account sits live and unused for three weeks, open to anyone who obtains that password before the teacher arrives.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the jobs match. But the predecessor may hold leftover rights; the approved role, not another person's access, sets what the teacher gets.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one standard password is simple. But anyone who knows it can sign in as any new hire; first credentials must be unique.

tips: Eliminate: D gives new hires a guessable standard first password, and C copies another person's rights instead of the approved role.
Final two: B beats A because access should go live when it is needed; a unique password still leaves an enabled, unused account open for three weeks.
Exam cue: provision from the trusted record, give the approved role only, and switch access on when the person actually starts.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management); CIS Controls v8.1 Safeguard 6.1 (Establish an Access Granting Process)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'provision from the trusted record and enable access when the person starts' (notes 3.1.3 Provisioning and Identity Proofing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An orchestra's AI sign-in scoring blocks dozens of musicians on a foreign tour, and the security analyst confirms the sign-ins are genuine; security management sets the risk thresholds. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Leave the blocks, since AI scoring errs on the side of caution
options.B: Raise the risk threshold so sign-ins from the tour countries pass
options.C: Ask security management to switch off the scoring until the tour ends
options.D: Report the false alarms to security management with the tour dates

questions.key_concept: Confirmed false alarms from AI risk scoring go to the threshold owner for tuning; the analyst reports, the owner retunes.
questions.pre_read: Note who sets the thresholds and what the analyst has already established.
questions.correct_explanation: AI scoring errs both ways, so confirmed false alarms go back to whoever owns the thresholds. Reporting them, with the tour dates as evidence, lets security management retune the model for travel. Raising the threshold is the runner-up: it would unblock the musicians, but it changes a setting the analyst does not own and, loosened for whole countries, could let real attackers through.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because caution feels safe. But blocking genuine users is a real failure too; confirmed false alarms should be fed back so the model is tuned.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a higher threshold would unblock the musicians. But security management sets thresholds, and loosening them for whole countries could pass real attackers too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it ends the disruption fast. But switching off scoring removes a layer for everyone; the fix is tuning, not turning the control off.

tips: Eliminate: C removes the control for everyone instead of tuning it, and A accepts confirmed false alarms instead of feeding them back.
Final two: D beats B because thresholds belong to security management; the analyst reports the evidence and the owner retunes.
Exam cue: AI scoring needs human feedback. Send confirmed false alarms, with evidence, to whoever owns the thresholds instead of retuning it yourself.

questions.question: A zoo keeper joins the education team today, the animal records owner approved no handover access, and the mover procedure has the access analyst remove old-role rights that day. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Remove the keeper's animal records rights and close the ticket
options.B: Keep the records rights open in case the old team needs help
options.C: Disable the keeper's whole account today until the new role is set
options.D: Ask the animal records owner to confirm the rights can be removed

questions.key_concept: At a job change, old access is removed at the move; when the procedure assigns that task, the analyst does it.
questions.pre_read: Note what the owner has already decided, and what the procedure asks the analyst to do.
questions.correct_explanation: A transfer is a leaver plus a joiner: old access goes at the move. Here the procedure gives the analyst that task, and the owner approved no handover access, so removing the rights today and recording it is in role. Asking the owner to confirm is the runner-up: owners decide exceptions, but the decision is already made, and waiting leaves old access live.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because helping old colleagues is common. But kept rights build privilege creep; a real handover need is approved separately, with an end date.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is cautious. But it blocks the keeper's new work too; a mover keeps their account and changes only its access.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the owner decides on old access. But the owner already approved no handover, and the procedure assigns removal to the analyst, so asking again only delays it.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps old rights just in case, which builds privilege creep, and C treats a job change as an exit and blocks the new work.
Final two: A beats D because the procedure assigns removal to the analyst and the owner already decided; asking again only delays it.
Exam cue: when the procedure gives you the task and the owner's decision is on record, act in role; escalate only what is outside it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-5 (Personnel Transfer); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'remove old access at the move, not later' (notes 3.1.9 Movers and Privilege Creep). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A port authority's quarterly access review closed Friday with 14 lines the harbor systems owner never confirmed, and the review procedure has the analyst running it remove unconfirmed access. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Mark the 14 lines as kept, since the owner raised no objection
options.B: Ask each of the 14 users whether to remove their access
options.C: Remove access on the 14 lines, then inform the owner
options.D: Extend the deadline and ask the owner to decide before any removal

questions.key_concept: In an access review, access the owner does not confirm is removed; the review is done when the removals are.
questions.pre_read: Note what the review procedure says happens to unconfirmed lines, and whom it assigns.
questions.correct_explanation: Access nobody confirms is removed, and here the procedure assigns that removal to the analyst running the review. Removing the 14 accesses and telling the owner keeps the review meaningful; the owner can re-request anything truly needed. Extending the deadline is the runner-up: chasing the owner seems polite, but the procedure has already set the outcome, and each extension leaves unconfirmed access live.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because silence looks like consent. But treating no answer as approval turns the review into a rubber stamp; unconfirmed access is removed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because users know what they use. But self-review is a conflict of interest; the accountable owner, not the user, confirms access.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: owners do decide who keeps access. But the deadline passed, the procedure says unconfirmed access goes, and extensions leave it live; the owner can re-request.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the owner's silence as approval, and B lets users review their own access, which is a conflict of interest.
Final two: C beats D because the procedure already says unconfirmed access goes; chasing the owner again keeps that access live.
Exam cue: in an access review, access nobody confirms is removed. If the procedure gives you that step, do it and inform the owner.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'access nobody confirms in a review is removed' (notes 3.1.10 Access Reviews and Recertification). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D3 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: An aquarium's governance tool flags every right unused for 90 days, including the life-support system's emergency override role, which is used only in twice-yearly drills. What is the review analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Remove every flagged right automatically, then inform each owner
options.B: Send the flagged rights to their owners to decide line by line
options.C: Keep every flagged right and widen the idle window to a year
options.D: Ask each flagged user to confirm which rights they still need

questions.key_concept: Usage reports inform access reviews, but they show what is used, not what is needed; the owner decides each line.
questions.pre_read: Ask what 'unused for 90 days' can and cannot tell you about whether a right is needed.
questions.correct_explanation: Usage data shows what is used, not what is needed. A right used only in emergencies can look idle for months and still be essential, so each owner decides line by line. Removing every flagged right and then informing owners is the runner-up: it applies least privilege quickly and keeps owners told, but they hear only after the emergency override the life-support system depends on is gone.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: removing idle rights usually supports least privilege, and owners are told. But only after removal, so the drill-only override could be gone in a life-support failure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids removing the drill-only override. But it keeps every idle right open to attackers; most flagged rights should go once the owner decides.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because users know their own work. But self-review is a conflict of interest; owners, not users, confirm who keeps access.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps every idle right that attackers could still use, and D lets users approve their own rights.
Final two: B beats A because usage shows what is used, not what is needed; owners told after removal cannot save the drill-only override.
Exam cue: usage reports inform an access review, but the owner decides. Watch for rights that are rare by design, such as emergency access.

questions.question: A radio station's IT technician has disabled a departing producer's account and ended its sessions, but the producer still has the station laptop, whose unencrypted drive holds recordings. What should the technician arrange as BEST?

options.A: Wipe the laptop remotely the next time it connects to the network
options.B: Rely on the disabled account, since the laptop asks for a sign-in
options.C: Let the producer keep the laptop once they delete the recordings
options.D: Have the laptop collected from the producer before they leave

questions.key_concept: Deprovisioning includes recovering company devices a leaver holds, because disabling the account does not protect an unencrypted drive.
questions.pre_read: List every way the producer could still reach the recordings after leaving.
questions.correct_explanation: Deprovisioning covers what a leaver holds, not just their account. A disabled account stops new sign-ins, but anyone who removes an unencrypted drive can read it, so the laptop must be collected before the producer leaves. A remote wipe is the runner-up: it is a useful backstop, but it runs only if the laptop connects again, and the recordings can be copied offline first.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a remote wipe is a good backstop. But it runs only if the laptop connects again, and the unencrypted recordings can be copied offline before then.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the account is disabled. But the sign-in screen guards only the operating system; an unencrypted drive can be removed and read elsewhere.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems fair to a departing colleague. But nobody can confirm the deletion, and company equipment goes back at exit.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts a sign-in screen to guard an unencrypted drive, and C relies on a leaver's word that the data is gone.
Final two: D beats A because collecting the laptop ends the exposure at exit; a remote wipe waits for a connection that may never come.
Exam cue: deprovisioning covers the account, its sessions and tokens, and what the leaver holds: devices, badges and any secret they knew.

questions.question: A game studio's HR director asks the IT technician to delete a dismissed developer's account at once, but the leaver procedure keeps accounts 90 days before deletion. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Reset the password and pass the account to the developer's team
options.B: Delete the account now, since HR set the developer's end date
options.C: Disable the account now and delete it when the 90 days end
options.D: Leave the account active until the 90 days have passed

questions.key_concept: Leaver accounts are disabled at once and deleted later under the retention rule, so logs still trace to the person.
questions.pre_read: Separate stopping the developer's access from deciding when the account record goes.
questions.correct_explanation: Disable first, delete later: disabling stops all use at once, while keeping the account for the retention period preserves the link between logs and the person and protects data that may still be needed. Deleting at once is the runner-up: it looks safest and the HR director asked, but HR sets the end date, not how IT removes accounts, and deletion can lose evidence.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the team still needs the developer's files. But a reused login cannot show who acted; reassign the data, not the account.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: deletion looks final, and HR asked. But HR sets the end date, not the method; deleting now can lose data and break the log trail.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the account must be kept 90 days. But kept is not active: a dismissed person's account must stop working at once.

tips: Eliminate: D confuses keeping the account with keeping it usable, and A turns a leaver's login into a shared account.
Final two: C beats B because disabling stops access now and keeps the log trail; deleting at once can lose data and evidence.
Exam cue: for leavers, disable at once and delete later under the retention rule; never reuse the account.

questions.question: A crowdfunding platform's AI support agent calls the payments application programming interface (API) with a key written into its source code, which 40 developers can read. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Replace the key and store the new one in a vault
options.B: Rotate the key every month but keep it in the source code
options.C: Encode the key in the code so readers cannot recognize it
options.D: Have the agent use a developer's personal key instead

questions.key_concept: Machine secrets such as API keys belong in a vault, not in code, and are replaced once exposed.
questions.pre_read: Count who can read the key today under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Secrets belong in a vault, not in code, and a key already seen by 40 people should be replaced. Issuing a new key and storing it in a vault that only the agent's identity can read closes the exposure and limits who can see it. Monthly rotation is the runner-up: rotation helps, but each new key would again sit in code that 40 developers can read.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: rotation limits how long a key is useful. But each new key would sit in readable code again, so the exposure never closes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the key no longer looks like a key. But encoding is reversible by anyone; it is not protection.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the developer's key already works. But the agent would act as that person, with their rights; non-human identities need their own credentials.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on encoding, which anyone can reverse, and D borrows a person's credential for an AI agent.
Final two: A beats B because a vault takes the key out of readable code; rotating a key that stays in code keeps exposing it.
Exam cue: machine secrets need their own identity, a vault and replacement after exposure; they are never written into code.

questions.question: A pension fund plans to buy an identity governance platform; today, access is copied from coworkers and approved by whoever is free. What should the IT analyst advise FIRST?

options.A: Choose the platform with the most connectors to other systems
options.B: Define the job roles and an owner for each system before setup
options.C: Let the vendor's consultants act as owners who approve access
options.D: Set up the platform first and let its reports show needed roles

questions.key_concept: IAM tools automate the process they are given, so roles and accountable owners must be defined before the tool is set up.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the platform would automate if it went live today.
questions.correct_explanation: A tool automates whatever process it is given. Access copied from coworkers and approved by whoever is free means no defined roles and no accountable owners, so the platform would automate that mess. Defining roles and owners first gives it something sound to run. Setting up the platform first is the runner-up: its reports can help later, but without owners nobody can approve requests or act on what the reports show.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because connectors matter later. But choosing features before the process exists puts the tool first; it would still have nothing sound to run.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because consultants know the platform. But approvals belong to the fund's own owners, who are accountable for their data.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: platform reports can support analysis later. But without owners, nobody can approve requests or act on the findings; the process must come first.

tips: Eliminate: A picks a tool by features before the process exists, and C gives approval to outsiders who are not accountable for the data.
Final two: B beats D because the platform needs roles and owners to run approvals and reviews; reports nobody owns change nothing.
Exam cue: process and ownership come before tools. An IAM platform automates what it is given, good or bad.

questions.question: An opera house's production manager, who owns its rehearsal-scheduling tool, requests admin rights on it for themselves and approves their own ticket. What should the help desk analyst fulfilling it do FIRST?

options.A: Add the analyst's own approval to the ticket, then grant it
options.B: Grant the rights, since the tool's owner approved the request
options.C: Grant the rights, then tell the manager's supervisor afterward
options.D: Hold the ticket until the manager's supervisor approves it

questions.key_concept: Nobody approves their own access request, not even a resource owner; an independent approver signs off before anyone grants it.
questions.pre_read: Name who asked, who approved and who will grant, and check whether any two are the same person.
questions.correct_explanation: Nobody approves their own request, even the owner of the resource, because one person would then both ask and decide. The analyst holds the ticket until someone independent, such as the manager's supervisor, approves it, then fulfills it. Granting first and telling the supervisor afterward is the runner-up: the supervisor is the right check, but after-the-fact notice cannot stop an unsuitable grant.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it adds a second look. But the help desk fulfills requests; approving what it grants merges two duties that should stay apart.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because owners approve access to their tools. But here the owner is also the requester, and self-approval removes the independent check.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the supervisor is the right independent check. But telling them afterward only reports a grant already made; approval must come before access.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a self-approval because the requester owns the tool, and A lets the person granting access also approve it.
Final two: D beats C because approval must come before access; telling the supervisor afterward cannot stop an unsuitable grant.
Exam cue: in access requests, the requester, the approver and the person who grants must be different people, whatever their rank.

questions.question: A property company is drafting a three-year contract giving an elevator firm's technicians portal accounts, and technicians often leave mid-contract. Which clause should the IT analyst propose to BEST make sure leavers lose access?

options.A: Each technician account expires on the day the three-year contract ends
options.B: The elevator firm gets admin rights to manage its staff's accounts
options.C: The elevator firm reports each technician's departure within days
options.D: The elevator firm vets each technician before they get an account

questions.key_concept: An outsider's departure never reaches your HR records, so contracts require partners to report leavers promptly and sponsors act on each notice.
questions.pre_read: Picture a technician who leaves in the contract's first month, and trace when each clause ends their access.
questions.correct_explanation: Outside staff leave without the company's HR records showing it, so the contract must require the elevator firm to report each technician's departure within days; the company's sponsor then has that access removed. Expiry at contract end is the runner-up: matching access to the contract is good practice, but technicians often leave mid-contract, and a leaver would keep access until the contract ends.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: matching access to the contract is good practice. But a technician who leaves in month three keeps access until the contract ends, years later.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the firm would remove its own leavers. But portal admin rights let an outside firm, not the company's sponsor and owner, decide who gets and keeps accounts.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vetting is a common contract term. But it checks technicians when they start; it never tells the company when one leaves.

tips: Eliminate: B gives an outside firm admin rights to decide who has portal accounts, and D checks technicians at the start but says nothing about when they leave.
Final two: C beats A because technicians leave mid-contract; a leaver notice ends access within days, while contract-end expiry leaves it open for years.
Exam cue: your HR never sees an outsider leave, so contracts require partners to report leavers, and the sponsor acts on each notice.

questions.question: At a concert venue's box office, agents share one terminal, walk away without signing out, and the next agent sometimes acts in the still-open session. Which control should the IT technician propose as BEST?

options.A: Lock idle sessions so a fresh sign-in is needed to resume
options.B: Require a passkey to open each agent's session at shift start
options.C: Remind agents in training to sign out before leaving the desk
options.D: Log each sale and refund under the agent whose session is open

questions.key_concept: Session controls such as idle locks protect the time after sign-in, when an open session can be used by anyone at the screen.
questions.pre_read: Think about what protects an open session once the agent who started it walks away.
questions.correct_explanation: A session stays usable until it ends, so an unattended open session gives the next person the previous agent's access. A short idle lock that needs sign-in to resume closes most of that gap without relying on anyone's memory. Reminding agents to sign out is the runner-up: training helps, but at a busy counter people forget, and the control depends on memory rather than the system.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because passkeys are strong. But strong sign-in protects only the start; the open session afterward is what the next agent uses.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: signing out is the right habit. But at a busy counter people forget; a technical idle lock works even when someone does.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs record who acted. But the log names whoever opened the session, so it would blame the wrong agent and does nothing to stop the next one acting.

tips: Eliminate: D logs actions under whoever opened the session, which blames the wrong agent, and B strengthens the sign-in but leaves the open session unprotected.
Final two: A beats C because the lock works even when an agent forgets; training alone depends on memory at a busy counter.
Exam cue: sign-in protects the start of a session; idle locks, timeouts and reauthentication protect the hours after it.

questions.question: A seed bank's new inventory app lets any signed-in staff member open every screen that has not been specifically restricted. Which change is BEST for the security analyst to request from the vendor?

options.A: Add multifactor authentication to every staff member's sign-in
options.B: Deny by default, granting each screen only to roles that need it
options.C: Restrict access to each screen that holds sensitive inventory data
options.D: Log every screen each staff member opens, with user and time

questions.key_concept: Logical access controls start from default deny: anything not explicitly allowed is refused.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens to a screen nobody has thought about yet under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Logical access should start from default deny: anything not explicitly allowed is refused, and access is granted through roles or groups. That closes every screen, including ones added later, until someone grants it. Restricting the sensitive screens is the runner-up: it fixes today's obvious gaps, but it keeps the allow-by-default design, so any new or overlooked screen opens to everyone.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because multifactor authentication is strong. But it proves who signs in; it does not limit what a signed-in user may open.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it protects the screens known to be sensitive today. But everything else stays open by default, including screens added later.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs trace misuse. But accounting records access; it grants or blocks nothing.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens authentication, which proves identity but limits nothing after sign-in, and D adds accounting, which records access without blocking it.
Final two: B beats C because default deny covers every screen, new ones included; restricting a list leaves the rest open.
Exam cue: allow by default is the flaw; default deny is the fix. Authentication proves who, authorization limits what, accounting records it.
