questions.question: A marathon organizer's new chief executive asks IT for edit access to every system, to stay informed about operations. Which response should the IT manager propose as BEST?

options.A: A separate admin account for edits, beside their daily one
options.B: Full edit access, since a chief executive oversees every system
options.C: Full edit access, with every change logged and reviewed monthly
options.D: Read-only dashboards covering what the executive needs to follow

questions.key_concept: Least privilege gives each person, whatever their rank, only the access their task needs.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the executive wants to see from what they would need to change.
questions.correct_explanation: Least privilege gives the access a task needs, and rank is not a task. Staying informed needs visibility, not the power to change records, so read-only dashboards meet the need and limit damage if the executive's account is phished. Logged edit access is the runner-up: logs help trace misuse, but they record harm after it happens, and the executive's account stays a prized target.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because separate admin accounts are good practice. But staying informed needs no edits at all, so a second account only adds another privileged target.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because executives oversee everything. But overseeing is not editing, and senior accounts are prime targets for attackers.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: logging and review add oversight. But they detect misuse after it happens; the edit rights a phished account could abuse remain.

tips: Eliminate: B grants access by rank instead of task, and A adds a privileged account for edits the executive's task never needs.
Final two: D beats C because read-only access meets the need to stay informed; logging edit rights only detects misuse later.
Exam cue: least privilege applies to every rank. Match the access to the task's verb: viewing needs read, not edit.

questions.question: At an events company, a clerk enters payments and a manager approves them, but the clerk can still edit a payment after approval. Which assessment should the security analyst give as MOST accurate?

options.A: The duties are separated, since a manager approves every payment
options.B: The duties are combined, but logging the clerk's edits makes that acceptable
options.C: The duties are combined, since the clerk can alter approved payments
options.D: The duties are separated, since each person's account holds least privilege

questions.key_concept: Separation of duties holds only if no one person can complete the process alone, including by editing it after approval.
questions.pre_read: Count who can take a payment from entry to approval on their own.
questions.correct_explanation: Separation of duties works only if no one person can complete a sensitive process alone. Because the clerk can edit a payment after the manager approves it, the clerk alone still decides what is finally paid. Manager approval is the runner-up: it looks like a split, but an approval the clerk can change afterward checks nothing; edits after approval should need a fresh approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a manager does approve each payment. But the clerk can change the payment afterward, so the approval no longer controls what is paid.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because logs record each edit. But logging detects a change after it happens; it does not stop one person from deciding alone what is paid.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because each account is narrow. But least privilege limits what one account does; separation of duties makes sure no one person can finish the process alone.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts the combined duty because edits are logged, which detects but does not split, and D confuses least privilege with separation of duties.
Final two: C beats A because the clerk can still change a payment after approval; an approval one person can undo separates nothing.
Exam cue: test separation of duties by asking whether one person can still finish the task alone, including by changing it after the check.

questions.question: A cinema chain's admins check out passwords from a vault that logs each use, and a senior admin wants a permanent copy in a personal password manager. What should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Keep the password in the vault, checked out for each task
options.B: Allow the copy if multifactor authentication protects the password manager
options.C: Give admins one shared vault login so check-out is quicker
options.D: Allow the copy, since senior admins are already trusted with it

questions.key_concept: Privileged credentials stay in the vault, where each check-out is logged and controlled; personal copies escape that control.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the vault records each time a password is used, and what a copy would record.
questions.correct_explanation: A vault controls privileged passwords by checking them out for a task, logging each use and often rotating them afterward. A permanent copy outside the vault escapes all of that: its use is never logged, and it lasts until someone notices. Allowing the copy behind multifactor authentication is the runner-up: it protects the copy from theft, but it still removes the logging and control the vault provides.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: multifactor authentication guards the copy. But the vault's logging and control of each use are lost, and the copy outlives any rotation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it speeds check-out. But a shared vault login cannot show which admin took which password.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the senior admin is trusted. But privileged controls guard against stolen accounts and mistakes, not just distrust; seniority changes nothing.

tips: Eliminate: D relaxes privileged controls because of seniority, and C shares one vault login so check-outs cannot be traced to a person.
Final two: A beats B because the vault logs and controls every use; a protected copy outside it is still unlogged and permanent.
Exam cue: privileged credentials stay in the vault: checked out for a task, logged and rotated, never kept as personal copies.

questions.question: At an animation studio that uses discretionary access control, a designer opens a malicious attachment, and the malware reshares the designer's project files with an outside address. Which weakness does this MOST clearly show?

options.A: A central administrator set the files' labels too low
options.B: Any program a user runs acts with the user's sharing rights
options.C: The designer's job role held more permissions than needed
options.D: Owners often share files with more people than needed

questions.key_concept: Under discretionary access control, any program the owner runs, including malware, acts with the owner's rights to share and change files.
questions.pre_read: Trace each step from the attachment opening to the files being shared.
questions.correct_explanation: Under discretionary access control, the owner decides who may access their files, and any program the owner runs acts with those same rights. Malware launched by the designer could therefore reshare the files as if the designer had chosen to. Owner oversharing is the runner-up: it is a real weakness of the model, but here the designer made no sharing choice; the malware acted with their rights.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because labels control access in some models. But centrally set labels belong to mandatory access control, not to owner-decided sharing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because extra role rights cause harm. But job roles belong to role-based access control; here the file owner's own rights were used.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: oversharing is a classic weakness of this model. But the designer chose nothing here; the malware shared the files using the designer's rights.

tips: Eliminate: A describes labels from mandatory access control, and C describes job roles from role-based access control; neither fits owner-decided sharing.
Final two: B beats D because the designer shared nothing; malware ran with the owner's rights, which is the model's built-in weakness.
Exam cue: in discretionary access control, the owner's rights travel with whatever the owner runs, malware included.

questions.question: In a cruise line's role-based access control system, where role owners approve each role's rights, an access analyst finds 40 staff with permissions granted directly, outside any role. What should the analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep the grants, since the 40 staff use them every day
options.B: Remove the 40 direct rights now, then tell the role owners
options.C: Create a separate role for each of the 40 staff
options.D: Have role owners fold needed rights into roles or drop them

questions.key_concept: Role-based access control works when rights come through roles; the role owner decides whether a direct grant joins a role or goes.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can tell which of the direct grants are still needed.
questions.correct_explanation: Role-based access control works when rights come through roles; direct grants bypass the catalog and its reviews. The role owner decides whether each needed right belongs in a role, perhaps as a time-limited extra, or should go. Removing all 40 at once is the runner-up: it restores the model fast, but some grants may support live work, and the owner, not the analyst, decides that.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the access is in use. But use is not approval; direct grants escape role reviews and build privilege creep.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: direct grants should end. But some may support live work; the role owner decides which become role rights and which go, before removal.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it puts every right in a role. But one role per person is role explosion, which nobody can manage or review.

tips: Eliminate: A treats daily use as approval, and C creates one role per person, which is role explosion.
Final two: D beats B because the role owner decides which rights stay; removing all at once could cut access people need for live work.
Exam cue: in role-based access control, rights should flow through roles. Report direct grants to the role owner to fold in or remove.

questions.question: A mining company's rule blocks portal sign-ins from outside its two operating countries, and the rule's owner approved an exception for an engineer's trip to Chile. How should the access analyst BEST set it up?

options.A: Add Chile to the rule's allowed countries until the trip ends
options.B: Give this engineer a standing exception for Chile
options.C: Let this engineer sign in from Chile during the trip
options.D: Have this engineer use a consumer VPN app to appear in-country

questions.key_concept: An approved exception to an access rule is scoped to the need: only the person, place and period it covers, and then it expires.
questions.pre_read: For each option, note who could sign in, from where, and until when.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule-based access control applies one rule to everyone, so an exception should open only what the need requires. The owner approved one engineer's trip, so the analyst sets an exception for this engineer, from Chile, ending with the trip. Adding Chile to the rule until the trip ends is the runner-up: it is limited by place and time, but it changes the rule for every user, not just the engineer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it covers only Chile and ends with the trip. But editing the rule accepts sign-ins from Chile for every user; the owner approved an exception for one engineer.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the engineer may travel again. But a permanent exception outlives the approved need; each future trip gets its own approval.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it needs no rule change. But a consumer VPN disguises where the engineer really is, going around the owner's rule instead of using the exception the owner approved.

tips: Eliminate: D disguises the engineer's location with a consumer VPN to get around the rule, and B makes a one-trip exception permanent.
Final two: C beats A because the owner approved an exception for one person; changing the rule itself opens Chile to every user.
Exam cue: scope an approved exception to the person, place and period the need covers, and let it expire on its own.

questions.question: A city records office uses role-based access control for its applications, and staff now want to share low-sensitivity working folders with colleagues they choose. Which approach should the security analyst advise as BEST?

options.A: Discretionary control for the folders, role-based control for the apps
options.B: Role-based access control for both, adding a role for each sharing need
options.C: Mandatory access control for both, since it is the strictest model
options.D: Discretionary access control for folders and apps, so owners grant both

questions.key_concept: Organizations mix access control models, using each where it fits the data and who should decide.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should decide access to the folders, and who should decide access to the applications.
questions.correct_explanation: Organizations mix models, choosing each where it fits. Low-sensitivity working folders suit discretionary access control, where the owner shares with chosen colleagues, while applications stay under role-based access control. Forcing everything into roles is the runner-up: it keeps one model, but a role for every sharing choice leads to role explosion, and nobody could manage or review the result.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: one model sounds tidy. But a role for every sharing choice causes role explosion; owner-decided sharing fits low-sensitivity folders better.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is the strictest model. But mandatory access control is rigid and costly; it suits classified data, not working folders.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners know their data. But owner-decided access to business applications breaks the job-based control those systems need.

tips: Eliminate: C picks the strictest model rather than the one that fits, and D lets folder owners decide application access too.
Final two: A beats B because mixing models is normal; forcing ad hoc sharing into roles creates role explosion.
Exam cue: choose the model per system by who should decide and how sensitive the data is; most organizations combine models.

questions.subtopic: 3.2 Logical access. Automated systems and AI agents
questions.question: A solar installer's AI agent only reads supplier invoices and drafts payment entries, yet its account can also change supplier bank details. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep the right, since the agent's vendor is well regarded
options.B: Remove the agent's right to change supplier bank details
options.C: Alert finance staff whenever the agent changes supplier bank details
options.D: Scan each invoice for viruses before the agent reads it

questions.key_concept: AI agents get only the rights their task needs; removing an unneeded right beats detecting its misuse.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the agent's task needs with what its account can do.
questions.correct_explanation: An agent should hold only the rights its task needs. Reading invoices and drafting entries never requires changing bank details, so removing that right means a hidden instruction in a crafted invoice, or a model error, cannot redirect payments. Real-time alerts are the runner-up: they speed up detection, but a redirected payment may already be on its way, and a right the task never needs should not exist.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a trusted vendor built it. But a manipulated or faulty agent misuses whatever rights it holds, whoever made it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: alerts speed up detection. But a redirected payment may already be sent; a right the task never needs should simply be removed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because invoices come from outside. But the risk here is excess rights that crafted text could trigger, which a virus scan does not address.

tips: Eliminate: D applies a malware scan to an excess-rights problem, and A trusts the vendor's reputation instead of limiting the agent's rights.
Final two: B beats C because a right the agent lacks cannot be misused; an alert only reports a change already made.
Exam cue: scope each bot or AI agent to its task. Removing unneeded rights prevents misuse; alerts only detect it.

questions.question: An ice arena evacuates after an ammonia alarm; ventilation needs admin rights, the system owner is unreachable, and the runbook lets the supervisor use break-glass access for life safety. What should the supervisor do FIRST?

options.A: Keep calling the owner to approve the break-glass use
options.B: Start the ventilation with the on-call engineer's admin login
options.C: Ask the help desk to make the supervisor a permanent administrator
options.D: Use the break-glass account to start the ventilation

questions.key_concept: When lives are at risk and the runbook authorizes break-glass access, use it at once; alerting and review follow.
questions.pre_read: Note what the runbook allows, and whom it allows to act.
questions.correct_explanation: People's safety comes first, and the runbook already authorizes break-glass access for life-safety events, so the supervisor acts now. Every break-glass use raises an alert, is reviewed afterward, and the credential is changed. Calling the owner for approval is the runner-up: owner approval is normal for elevation, but the runbook has already granted it for this case, and each minute of delay lets the leak build while people are still near the building.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: elevation normally needs the owner's approval. But the runbook already authorizes the supervisor's break-glass use for life-safety events, and each minute of waiting lets the ammonia build.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is quick. But a borrowed personal login cannot show who acted and bypasses the sealed, alerted emergency path.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it would prevent future delays. But standing admin rights help attackers too, and the help desk cannot fix tonight's emergency in time.

tips: Eliminate: B borrows another person's login instead of the sealed emergency path, and C answers an emergency with permanent admin rights.
Final two: D beats A because lives are at risk and the runbook already authorizes break-glass use; the review comes after.
Exam cue: people's safety comes first. When a procedure already authorizes the emergency action, act on it, then record and review.

questions.question: A biotech company labels its clinical trial files Restricted, but each study leader may grant any colleague access to their own study's files at will. Which model should the access analyst MOST accurately record?

options.A: Role-based access control, since study leaders hold a defined job role
options.B: Mandatory access control, since the files carry Restricted labels
options.C: Discretionary access control, since study leaders choose who gets in
options.D: Attribute-based access control, as the Restricted label is an attribute

questions.key_concept: Name the access control model by who decides access; labels that no system enforces do not make it mandatory.
questions.pre_read: Find who actually decides whether a colleague may open a study's file.
questions.correct_explanation: Read for the decider. Labels alone do not make a system mandatory: under mandatory access control, the system enforces labels against clearances and no owner can override them. Here each study leader grants access at will, so the owner decides, which is discretionary. Mandatory access control is the runner-up, because the Restricted label is the eye-catching clue, but nothing enforces it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because study leaders hold a job title. But nothing here grants access by job role; each study leader personally chooses who gets in.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: labels suggest mandatory control. But under that model the system enforces labels against clearances, and no study leader could grant access at will.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a label can be an attribute. But no policy checks it on each request; the study leader's choice alone decides.

tips: Eliminate: A confuses a job title with access granted by role, and D treats a label as a checked attribute when no policy evaluates it.
Final two: C beats B because the study leader decides access at will; a label nobody enforces does not make a model mandatory.
Exam cue: name the model by who decides, not by what the data is called. If the owner can grant at will, it is discretionary.
